short_definition: A market correction is a drop of roughly 10% to 20% from a recent peak in a stock index or asset price, short of the 20% decline often labeled a bear market.
explanation: A market correction is measured from the most recent high to the lowest point that follows. The 10% and 20% thresholds are informal conventions used by financial media and analysts, not official rules. A correction can happen within days or unfold over months. Common triggers include interest-rate changes, disappointing earnings, weak economic data or prices that had risen faster than fundamentals.

Corrections matter because they are a normal part of investing in stocks and have occurred periodically, including during long-term uptrends. Knowing the term helps you put alarming headlines in context. It also helps you test whether your portfolio and risk tolerance hold up when prices actually fall.

The main risk is behavioral. Nobody can reliably predict when a correction will start, when it will end or whether it will turn into a bear market. Selling in a panic can lock in losses. Buying the dip with money you need soon can backfire if prices keep falling. Past patterns don't guarantee future results.
example: Illustrative example: An index closes at a record 5,000 points, then falls to 4,400 over six weeks. That is a 600-point drop, or 12% (600 ÷ 5,000), which fits the correction label. If it kept falling to 3,900, a 22% drop from the peak, commentators would usually call it a bear market.
common_mistake: Treating every correction as a signal to sell everything. Investors who move to cash after a drop often lock in losses and then struggle to decide when to get back in.
title: Market Correction
